content: Ferromagnetism is the most commonly recognized form of magnetism, as seen in objects like horseshoe magnets and refrigerator magnets. It is the primary type of magnetism encountered in everyday life. The attraction between a magnet and ferromagnetic materials was one of the earliest observed magnetic phenomena, both in ancient times and today. Ferromagnetism is defined as the property of certain materials, such as iron, to become magnetized in the presence of an external magnetic field and to retain this magnetization even after the external field is removed. All permanent magnets are either ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic, as are metals that are strongly attracted to magnets. Historically, the term ferromagnet referred to any material capable of exhibiting spontaneous magnetization, meaning a net magnetic moment in the absence of an external magnetic field. This broad definition is still widely used. However, more recent studies have identified different classes of spontaneous magnetization, particularly in materials with more than one magnetic ion per primitive cell. This has led to a stricter definition of ferromagnetism, distinguishing it from ferrimagnetism. Specifically, a material is considered ferromagnetic in this narrower sense only if all its magnetic ions contribute positively to the net magnetization. If some magnetic ions partially oppose the net magnetization (due to partial anti-alignment), the material is classified as ferrimagnetic. If the ions are completely anti-aligned, resulting in zero net magnetization despite magnetic ordering, the material is termed antiferromagnetic. These alignment effects occur only below a critical temperature, known as the Curie temperature for ferromagnets and ferrimagnets, or the Néel temperature for antiferromagnets. There are numerous crystalline materials that exhibit ferromagnetism or ferrimagnetism. Ferromagnetic metal alloys, whose individual components are not ferromagnetic in their pure forms, are called Heusler alloys, named after Fritz Heusler. Additionally, amorphous (non-crystalline) ferromagnetic metallic alloys can be created by rapidly cooling a liquid alloy. These materials have nearly isotropic properties, resulting in low coercivity, low hysteresis loss, high permeability, and high electrical resistivity. A typical example is a transition metal-metalloid alloy, composed of approximately 80% transition metal (such as Fe, Co, or Ni) and a metalloid component (such as B, C, Si, P, or Al) that lowers the melting point. A relatively new class of exceptionally strong ferromagnetic materials is rare-earth magnets, which contain lanthanide elements known for their ability to carry large magnetic moments in well-localized f-orbitals. The phenomenon of ferromagnetism arises from two quantum mechanical effects: electron spin and the Pauli exclusion principle. The spin of an electron, combined with its orbital angular momentum, creates a magnetic dipole moment and generates a magnetic field. In ferromagnetic materials, unpaired electron spins can align to produce a net magnetic moment even in the absence of an external field. When these spins align, they create a measurable macroscopic magnetic field. These permanent dipoles, often referred to as spins, tend to align parallel to an external magnetic field, a behavior known as paramagnetism. Ferromagnetism, however, involves an additional phenomenon: the dipoles tend to align spontaneously without any applied field. This is a purely quantum mechanical effect. Classical electromagnetism predicts that two nearby magnetic dipoles would align in opposite directions, creating an antiferromagnetic material. However, in ferromagnets, the Pauli exclusion principle causes the dipoles to align in the same direction. This principle states that two electrons with the same spin cannot occupy the same position, effectively reducing the energy of their electrostatic interaction compared to electrons with opposite spins. This energy difference is called the exchange energy. At long distances, the exchange energy advantage is overtaken by the classical tendency of dipoles to anti-align. This is why, in an equilibrated (non-magnetized) ferromagnetic material, the dipoles are not aligned across the entire material. Instead, they organize into magnetic domains (also known as Weiss domains) that are aligned at short range, but adjacent domains are anti-aligned at long range. The boundaries between these domains are known as domain walls (e.g., Bloch or Néel walls, depending on whether the magnetization rotates parallel or perpendicular to the domain interface) and represent a gradual transition on the atomic scale, covering a distance of about 300 ions for iron. As a result, an ordinary piece of iron generally has little or no net magnetic moment. However, if it is placed in a sufficiently strong external magnetic field, the domains will reorient in parallel with the field and remain reoriented when the field is removed, creating a permanent magnet. This magnetization as a function of the external field is described by a hysteresis curve. Although this state of aligned domains is not the lowest-energy configuration, it is extremely stable and has been observed to persist for millions of years in seafloor magnetite aligned by the Earth's magnetic field (whose poles can flip at long intervals). The net magnetization can be destroyed by heating and then cooling (annealing) the material without an external field. As temperature increases, thermal oscillation (entropy) competes with the ferromagnetic tendency for dipoles to align. When the temperature rises beyond a critical point, called the Curie temperature, a second-order phase transition occurs, and the system can no longer maintain spontaneous magnetization, although it still responds paramagnetically to an external field. Below the Curie temperature, spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs, and random domains form in the absence of an external field. The Curie temperature itself is a critical point where magnetic susceptibility theoretically becomes infinite, and domain-like spin correlations fluctuate at all length scales. The study of ferromagnetic phase transitions, particularly through simplified models like the Ising spin model, has significantly influenced the development of statistical physics. It was in this context that it became clear that mean field theory approaches failed to predict the correct behavior at the critical point, which was found to belong to a universality class that includes many other systems, such as liquid-gas transitions. This failure necessitated the development of renormalization group theory. Unusual forms of ferromagnetism have also been proposed in materials such as isoelectronic compounds of boron and nitrogen, which may exhibit ferromagnetic properties at extremely low temperatures, such as 5 K.
